utterances.text: And was ULT a term by which you understood that machine on the right back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And -- and how is it that you are familiar with these pieces of machinery and their names and functions?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know these machines because of a company, GP Radnik, which operated in Srebrenica and which used these machines, and I was able to see them in construction works on the coast and on -- in other construction sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to belabour this point any further. I think everybody knows what an excavator and a bulldozer is. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you able to see the colour of either of those vehicles, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're usually manufactured in -- they come in yellow colours, shades of yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That evening, sir, were you able to see what colour the vehicles were?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. They were probably yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as you and Mr. Suljic were escaping from the meadow, what could you see of the surrounding area, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were running away through the forest, we didn't see anything in particular. We were running away. When we turned, we could see the meadow. And when I was walking over the bodies, that was really horrible. It was filled with dead bodies, the meadow. And as I stood up, I turned around and I saw railway tracks, the embankment of the railway tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And along with Mr. Suljic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer, again. He hasn't told us so far what time of the evening or night he finally decided to stand up and together with Suljic took off.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the next question: When he decided to take off with Suljic, were there any Serbs or any movement on the part of the Serbs at the time? Because they decided even to talk amongst themselves in an open space like that, even a whisper would be heard. So if you could cover these.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you waited for the people that you heard talking amongst themselves leave until you decided to stand up. Did you see, other than Mr. Suljic and the two wounded people that you saw, any other living people before you decided to escape?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't see anybody. Nobody was there. And there were no Serb soldiers either. There were only the two of us, me and Suljic, and two wounded people who were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified that it was night, that it was cloudy but there was still some moon that was shining. Do you have any idea what time of the evening it was when you and Mr. Suljic finally made your way off of that meadow?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the cold, I can conclude that it was late, that it was past midnight, because past midnight the night becomes very cold so I had to put on my shirt. I was even cold once I had put on my shirt, and that makes me conclude that it was very late. I didn't see the time, but I can judge by these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection how long it took for the sun to rise after you and Mr. Suljic left the meadow?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came up to a torched house, we hid in the bushes. We went to sleep. I don't know how late it was, but when we woke up in the bushes the sun was already up there and it was already warm. We came up to a hill. We could see villages around, inhabited villages, Karakaj and others. I couldn't tell you what time it was when we woke up, but when we came up the hill we heard someone crying out for help. I don't know who it was. I couldn't see because of the forest, but somebody said, "Where are you going?" And they cursed. And then we started running away because we were very close to this spot. We came to a pear tree. We stopped there. Hurem went up and tried to pick some fruits, and then an elderly person came up to us. He was in civilian clothes, covered in blood. He emerged in front us. I asked him who he was, and he said that his name was Smajil Hodzic Cerski, and I asked him what happened. And then he said there was a firing squad, that there was shooting nearby, that he had survived and during the night he was able to run away, because the lights did not lit him. And he was somewhere in the corner, so that during the shooting he was able to run away. He was close to the forest. He went through the forest. And he entered a tunnel. He went through the tunnel, and then he was ambushed near Kalesija, and then he came up to where we were, and then the three of us set off together. We didn't know the way. We were just going.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did yourself and those two men eventually make your way to free territory, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. On the 21st of July, we came to Nezuk on the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. We'll have a 20-minute break now, and then we start with the cross-examination, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've been informed that Madam Fauveau would like to address the Chamber on a procedural matter. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, during the previous session I completely by chance fell on an interview that -- the interview of the witness that we have before you, the interview that was granted by this person to a Bosniak newspaper. I cannot read the ERN number, however, but this interview was never communicated to us. So this document, we only have it in Serbo-Croatian for now, and I believe a lot of my colleagues have not seen this document. I don't know if the accused has seen it, but I would like to ask for my colleagues that will start the cross-examination today, I would like to ask you to adjourn the cross-examination for tomorrow so that we can all read this interview and that the accused can also read this interview and know what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the Prosecution first and then we deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have very good communication with Ms. Fauveau. She has told us about her finding. We can't track it because of -- we can't read the ERN, but we don't know about this document. We have done thorough searches to find this kind of thing, and when we have newspaper articles that are significant like interviews, we always turn them over. So given it's late, given the witness is obviously getting tired and the time estimates of cross and the next witness, I don't see that we lose too much if we quit and put Mr. Ruez off for Wednesday, which I think is going to happen anyway if we go -- the following Wednesday, because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I think all in all we'll figure out where this thing came from, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have the problem or three-fourths of the problem solved, and I thank you for the way you have approached it, Mr. McCloskey. At the same time, it doesn't seem to be fully solved, because you haven't been able to track this document so far. And, Madam Fauveau, are you in possession of it? Because you seem to know even the language, that it is solely in the Bosnian, Serbo-Croat language.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have it in my computer only. I looked at it very briefly. I did not read the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how come -- you have it on your computer as part of the e-court filings or outside that? Is it part of the EDS?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's part of the EDS system, but it is not in the Srebrenica collection. It's in the general collection. The general collection is a series of documents that we usually do not consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And can I make a suggestion, therefore. If you perhaps can liaise. We will be adjourning. I suppose there is no ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The prevalent view here is that of course without prejudice to addressing this matter fully and reserving the rights of each and every Defence team to put relevant questions that we try not to lose this hour, what's left of it. We try to proceed with -- with the cross-examination -- with the first, at least, cross-examination and maybe the second, with the understanding that of course if we manage to find this document, and -- not, rather, we, if Prosecution finds this document, makes it available to all Defence counsel, then both Mr. Zivanovic and you, Mr. Meek, will be able to come back with further questions if at all necessary. I mean, because it all depends also on the content of this. In the meantime, Madam Fauveau, if you could perhaps liaise with Mr. Thayer or Mr. McCloskey and give more specific details which would enable them to find it, because if it's there in the EDS, they'll find it. I mean, it's there for everyone. Can I count on your cooperation, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring the witness, see what we can do for today, and then tomorrow we'll take this up. In the meantime, please try to locate this document, assuming it's the same person we're talking about. I wouldn't imagine there are many Mevludin Orics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Oric, once more. Now, Mr. Zivanovic, who has just stood up, is counsel, lead counsel, to accused Popovic, Vujadin Popovic, and he will be the first one to cross-examine you. Then we continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Oric. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I represent Vujadin Popovic in this case. I would like to take you back to Bratunac on the 14th of July, 1995, at the time when the convoy of vehicles was formed in order to transport you and other detainees towards Zvornik. Before that, you were on one of the four buses parked in front of the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The four buses then moved in front of the Vihor garage.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the parking lot of the Vihor company for the vehicles that were written off. This was not the main parking lot. There you could see some written-off trailers, obsolete vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you. You waited for an APC, a white APC bearing the marking of the United Nations that put itself at the head of that convoy, and then you started moving after this APC towards Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Oric, since you speak the same language, please allow a very short pause between question and answer, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, you were mobilised into the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This happened after the war was declared by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were the commander of a unit there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of a squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, 1995, you found yourself in Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 11th of July, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And on the 12th of July, in the morning, you were also in Susnjari, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of July I was in Jaglici from where we headed off towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Early in the morning on the 12th of July, you were grouped into brigades?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the 11th of July in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said something else previously, but let's skip that. Your unit was given the task to be at the rear of that column that had been formed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brigade and my neighbours belonged to the rear of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it have a certain task to maybe protect the rear of the column?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our order was to move in single file and not to step out because of the minefields, and there was another unit, a unit with weapons who were at the very back of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were behind you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, behind you [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And their task was to protect the rear of the column?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were armed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you didn't have enough weapons, you took turn holding the weapons in combat. Those who would get tired would take a rest and the others would take the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That didn't happen? On the front line didn't you say that the weapons stayed there all the time and people took turns, but they were shooting from the same rifles?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the retreat with the column, did your unit suffer any losses?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What retreat are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were leaving Susnjari and Jaglici towards Tuzla. I'm referring to the convoy that was moving, and I'm asking you whether your units -- unit came under fire and whether it suffered any losses.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay with your unit all the time until you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You abandoned your unit?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- the unit just broke apart. Nobody knew where everybody was. We split into groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the group that surrendered, those were not just people from your unit, the group that surrendered together with you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were people from your unit?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was armed at the moment when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably remember having given certain statements to the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was sometime around the 22nd of July, and that was some week or so after the events.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the MUP in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember? Did you say to them the same thing that you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I may have told them something less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But nothing different?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't tell them then that you were all civilians, nothing else but civilians?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, civilians without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't say that you had been given the order to start moving by Ramiz Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did receive the order from Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't say that on the 22nd of July to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never asked me anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't ask you then. Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Zivanovic. And as I said earlier, if you wish to return to -- to the witness with your further cross-examination tomorrow you will be able to do so, provided it's limited to that document that Madam Fauveau has mentioned. Mr. Meek. The same applies to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, Mr. Meek is defending Mr. Beara. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Oric. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you for asking. I'm well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'd like to just clarify a few things about your service in the various armies. As I understand it, you first served in -- with the JNA. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that was for your mandatory service; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Subsequent to that -- and by the way, what year was that again?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1988, on the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The 19th of December, 1988 [Realtime transcript read in error, "1998"], is the day you started your service or finished your service?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day that I started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall the date you finished or completed that service, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I finished sometime in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just to assist. We have the year of 1998 on page 58, line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it should be 1988, not 1998. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you began on December 19, 1988 and completed in March of 1989; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you -- who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our commander was Hajrudin Grabovica. He was the commander of that artillery unit. He was captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, sorry to interrupt. Was the mandatory service for four months?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For four months? Was the mandatory service for four months, then, at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. It should have been a year, but I did not complete my service. When I first started my service, I was under age. I was not even 18, so they sent me home to return four years later and to complete my service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I take it that you had to fill out papers to join the JNA in 1988; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to fill out anything. I was just recruited. The papers arrived in Srebrenica. This was just the call-up paper asking me to report to the JNA for my compulsory service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At the time that you were called up for your compulsory service did you understand and realise that you were under age at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I appealed, but the appeal was not granted. I had to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So that I understand this well, you informed the powers that be that you were under age, but they said you must go into the army anyway, and then four months later they released you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I take it you never misrepresented your age to anybody to get into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Subsequent to that service, it's my understanding that you joined the Croatian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. When did you join the Croatian army, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992. I joined the MUP, the MUP of Croatia, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to point out. He never said he joined the Croatian army. He said he joined the police, the MUP in Croatia, and that he moved to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for that clarification. Subsequent -- and apparently that was only for -- they both clarified it. Thank you both for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I recognise Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall have to intervene. The witness did mention having joined the HV. I believe we should all refer to that part of his testimony, when he did mention joining the HV eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let him explain what he did and what he didn't. But yesterday, definitely he was referring to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, let me just ask you this: First, how long were you with the MUP in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even a month, and then I went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And during your one-month service with the MUP, what were your duties, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there in Capljina. We were there to prevent any looting of the houses there. During the combat activities, our order was to prevent any looting of the houses. This was our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, to clarify for the record, during the combat activities that would have been between which side, the Serbian army and the Croatian army, or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA were in the barracks, and on the other side there was all sorts of troops. I don't know exactly what troops were there when this combat was going on. I only know that people had moved out and that our task was to protect the houses from looting. Most probably those troops were HVO and the Croatian army, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, from the -- to clarify your last answer, were you protecting the homes from looting, which looting was being done by the HVO and the Croatian army? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anybody who intended to do the looting. There were a lot of civilians who remained in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I'm being very patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I know you are, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what's the relevance of all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll move on, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay of the thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What's your date of birth, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st of February, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: After you were with the MUP and had gone to Zagreb, then you joined the HVO in and around Capljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I arrived in Zagreb, I went to my uncle's place in Kutina, and from there I wanted to go back to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did at some point in time you join the HVO in Capljina and/or Mostar, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in Orasje for a month. That's when I tried to go to Tuzla. I was prevented from doing that. There were obstacles on the road, and that's why I had to spend a month in Orasje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, even though I don't know how relevant this is going to be, but if you were born on the 1st of February, 1970, and you were recruited in the JNA in December of 1988, how come that you maintain you were not 18 years old as yet? Because you would have been almost 19 years old, 19 years old less one month, or even less than a month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was two or three months short of being 18. In February, 1989, I would have been 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I will not belabour this point, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's your birth year again? Is it 1970 or 1971?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 1970, 7-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not labour it any further. It's back to you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you testified on the transcript page 56, line 13, you answered a question put to you by the Prosecutor, and the answer was: "Yes, he knew that I had gone to Croatia, that I was in HV for a while, and he knew that I had also served in my own army." And that was, I believe, speaking about your cousin Naser Oric. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Please tell me how long you were in the HV and what were your duties were.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the HV. I was with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Oric, approximately when you finished your duties in Capljina, when did you return to Bosnia, approximately the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in May or thereabouts in 1992. That's when I arrived in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you stay in Tuzla, or did you go on to some other location?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed for a short while, and then I went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you a member of any military group while you were in Tuzla after May, 1992, and prior to moving on to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Territorial Defence at that time. That's what it was called, and I was a member thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, in Tuzla; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you travelled from Tuzla to Srebrenica, did you go alone or were you accompanied by other persons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went with a neighbour of mine and a guide, and there were also some people from Zvornicka Kamenica. There were 40 or so, all of us together, but I didn't know who they were. They moved on to go to Zvornicka Kamenica and the three of us went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you upon your arrival in Srebrenica did you immediately join the ABiH army or any military organisation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I took some time to rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Approximately how much time did you take to rest, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I take it after 10 days you joined the ABiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's when I joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And what group or battalion did you join, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 281st Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the 281st Division?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the arrival of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And for the record, could you tell me approximately what month and year that would have been?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mid-April, 1993. I don't know the exact date, but it was sometime in mid-April of 1993 when UNPROFOR arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Subsequent to mid-April of 1993, after UNPROFOR had arrived, you again joined the ABiH army at some point. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when would that have been, sir, and what unit or brigade were you involved with?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigades were transferred into companies that patrolled the lines that were between UNPROFOR and Zupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, approximately what month and year would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall the month, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe sometime in May or June. The brigades were reorganised into companies, and since there were a lot of incursions by Serb units, we controlled the gaps between the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At some point you became the brigade commander of the 283rd Brigade of the ABiH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you become the commander of a brigade other than the 283rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a manoeuvre company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And when did you become the commander of that manoeuvre company?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in June, as I've just told you. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you stay -- did you stay in that capacity as the commander of the company until the 11th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you -- how many -- how many soldiers were in your company?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were nine soldiers and I was the tenth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And how many weapons did you have between you and your soldiers, sir, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one set of rifles which stayed on the line. We didn't take them home. We had only one rifle that we used to take home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Briefly, I want to clarify this. "A set of rifles." How many are in a set when you say a set?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you had 10 rifles that were always continuously being used by your company. Is that what I understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you had one rifle that you would take home, or each of your company members would take a rifle home when they went home?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only one rifle would be taken home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, again during this time period from 1993 up until July 11th of 1995, did most of the companies and brigades have these kind of rifles, one per -- one rifle per one soldier, as you did?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, taking you to the 11th of July of 1995, I understand your testimony to be that you learned of the fall of Srebrenica when you were with -- went to see your sister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at the house where she lived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And how -- what was the distance between that house, your sister's house, and Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She resided in Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, when you learned that Srebrenica had fallen, what was your first step, sir? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I headed towards my home to see about my family and where they would go, but before that I informed my people on the line that Srebrenica had fallen and that we were supposed to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And where were you supposed to withdraw to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To our houses, Susnjari, Lihovici. Try and find the command and see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who told you to withdraw to your houses?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told us. I said we should withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you told your company, the members of your company, to withdraw to their houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me and this Trial Chamber what happened to the 10 guns that you had when everybody started withdrawing to their homes on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These rifles were used before the attack on Srebrenica. After this, they were deployed along the line. That day we had come to assist because UNPROFOR had withdrawn, so we came unarmed. We had this one rifle, and we had some grenades, and the set of 10 rifles were used before prior to the attack on Srebrenica. Afterwards, they were deployed along the line, but there was also this gap where UNPROFOR were -- was placed, and we were ordered to try to maintain this area where UNPROFOR was positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you say that afterwards the 10 rifles were deployed along the line, can you be more specific and tell me where that line was and who you gave these 10 rifles to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 10 rifles were left behind at Buljim, because at the time we were taking a rest. This was our shift. And then we were told that we should maintain this line, and the weapons were left on the line. And we came back from our homes to try to -- to keep the line, to maintain the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, if I understand you, at the time on July 11, 1995, you and your company were on a rest. Am I correct so far?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a squad, not a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Your squad. You were on a rest; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is it a fair statement, sir, that when your squad would be on a rest your 10 rifles would be used by 10 other ABiH soldiers? Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it true that this was a normal course of activity at that location in and around that location in and around that time, that being that when a squad or a company having 10 rifles like you did went on a rest, those 10 rifles would be used by ABiH soldiers so they would always be continuously in use?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He just answered that question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, in your some of your statements and even your testimony, I'd like to know when you ceased being an ABiH soldier and when you became a civilian, in 1995 specifically in the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At the time that you were -- or that you surrendered in July of 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, were you a soldier or were you a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a civilian wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to take you back to the 11th of July, you've just testified under oath that you were a soldier with the ABiH army and that you were just on a rest. Your company was on a rest. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My squad was on a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you were a soldier and your squad was on a rest. Excuse me. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then you surrendered on the 12th of July, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was captured on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, between the 11th of July when you were the commander of your squad with 10 rifles, when did you resign being an ABiH soldier?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I headed off from Jaglici towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So was there anything that you needed to do? For example, notify your immediate commander that you were no longer an ABiH soldier?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand you, you just decided at one moment you wanted to become a civilian and that's what you did?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And as a civilian, is it normal to carry one or two grenades with you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is it normal as a civilian in Srebrenica, a Muslim civilian at that time of -- between the ages of 16 and 70 or 60 to carry grenades and be civilians?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So were you the exception to the rule, Mr. Oric, that would carry grenades and be a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried it with me in the woods in case I had to defend myself or to shoot myself, if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you got to Susnjari there was a big rally. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And around 10.00, maybe a little later, there had been a decision made that everybody should head towards Tuzla. Is that your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who made this decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you specifically name the command or commanders who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- the decision was made by Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Becirevic was a military commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ramiz Becirevic or some other Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was Ramiz Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So at 10.00 on -- approximately 10.00 on the 11th of July, 1995, you were still taking commands from a military commander in the ABiH army. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you've estimated there were approximately 15.000 other people who took that same command?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who were armed, the soldiers had to take command from our superiors, and the civilians were simply moving behind the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, whenever it's convenient for you, we need to stop in about two, three minutes' time maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you -- again, you've estimated -- yesterday, you testified that you estimated there were possibly a total of 15.000 in this column that headed towards Tuzla. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You being one of them, you were an ABiH soldier at that time you took the command and started in the column towards Tuzla; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you will have to agree with me that the majority of the men in that column were also ABiH soldiers who took that same command as you did and started moving towards Tuzla; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They received the same command, and we headed towards Tuzla, but many of them were unarmed. They were unarmed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oric, for today, and I'm sure I will have a few questions for you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Oric, we are going to stop here today. We will resume tomorrow afternoon, 2.15, like today. In the meantime, try to sort out this unidentified document problem. Thank you, and have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
